{"type":"stream_event","event":{"type":"content_block_start","index":6,"content_block":{"type":"tool_result","tool_use_id":"call_7d0f536ef9514267bb530116","content":"[{\"url\": \"https://bheisler.github.io/criterion.rs/book/analysis.html\", \"content\": \"## Analysis Process\\nThis page details the data collection and analysis process used by Criterion.rs. This is a bit more advanced than the user guide; it is assumed the reader is somewhat familiar with statistical concepts. In particular, the reader should know what bootstrap sampling means.\\nSo, without further ado, let's start with a general overview. Each benchmark in Criterion.rs goes through four phases:\\n* Warmup - The routine is executed repeatedly to fill the CPU and OS caches and (if applicable) give the JIT time to compile the code\\n* Measurement - The routine is executed repeatedly and the execution times are recorded\\n* Analysis - The recorded samples are analyzed and distilled into meaningful statistics, which are then reported to the user\\n* Comparison - The performance of the current run is compared to the stored data from the last run to determine whether it has changed, and if so by how much\\n## Warmup\\nThe first step in the process is warmup. In this phase, the routine is executed repeatedly to give the OS, CPU and JIT time to adapt to the new workload. This helps prevent things like cold caches and JIT compilation time from throwing off the measurements later. The warmup period is controlled by the `warm_up_time` value in the Criterion struct.\\nThe warmup period is quite simple. The routine is executed once, then twice, four times and so on until the total accumulated execution time is greater than the configured warm up time. The number of iterations that were completed during this period is recorded, along with the elapsed time.\\n## Measurement\\nThe measurement phase is when Criterion.rs collects the performance data that will be analyzed and used in later stages. This phase is mainly controlled by the `measurement_time` value in the Criterion struct.\\nThe measurements are done in a number of samples (see the `sample_size` parameter). Each sample consists of one or more (typically many) iterations of the routine. The elapsed time between the beginning and the end of the iterations, divided by the number of iterations, gives an estimate of the time taken by each iteration.\\nAs measurement progresses, the sample iteration counts are increased. Suppose that the first sample contains 10 iterations. The second sample will contain 20, the third will contain 30 and so on. More formally, the iteration counts are calculated like so:\\n`iterations = [d, 2d, 3d, ... Nd]`\\nWhere `N` is the total number of samples and `d` is a factor, calculated from the rough estimate of iteration time measured during the warmup period, which is used to scale the number of iterations to meet the configured measurement time. Note that `d` cannot be less than 1, and therefore the actual measurment time may exceed the configured measurement time if the iteration time is large or the configured measurement time is small.\\nNote that Criterion.rs does not measure each individual iteration, only the complete sample. The resulting samples are stored for use in later stages. The sample data is also written to the local disk so that it can be used in the comparison phase of future benchmark runs.\\n## Analysis\\nDuring this phase Criterion.rs calculates useful statistics from the samples collected during the measurement phase.\\n### Outlier Classification\\nThe first step in analysis is outlier classification. Each sample is classified using a modified version of Tukey's Method, which will be summarized here. First, the interquartile range (IQR) is calculated from the difference between the 25th and 75th percentile. In Tukey's Method, values less than (25th percentile - 1.5 * IQR) or greater than (75th percentile + 1.5 * IQR) are considered outliers. Criterion.rs creates additional fences at (25pct - 3 * IQR) and (75pct + 3 * IQR); values outside that range are considered severe outliers.\\nOutlier classification is important because the analysis method used to estimate the average iteration time is sensitive to outliers. Thus, when Criterion.rs detects outliers, a warning is printed to inform the user that the benchmark may be less reliable. Additionally, a plot is generated showing which data points are considered outliers, where the fences are, etc.\\nNote, however, that outlier samples are _not_ dropped from the data, and are used in the following analysis steps along with all other samples.\\n### Linear Regression\\nThe samples collected from a good benchmark should form a rough line when plotted on a chart showing the number of iterations and the time for each sample. The slope of that line gives an estimate of the time per iteration. A single estimate is difficult to interpret, however, since it contains no context. A confidence interval is generally more helpful. In order to generate a confidence interval, a large number of bootstrap samples are generated from the measured samples. A line is fitted to each of the bootstrap samples, and the result is a statistical distribution of slopes that gives a reliable confidence interval around the single estimate calculated from the measured samples.\\nThis resampling process is repeated to generate the mean, standard deviation, median and median absolute deviation of the measured iteration times as well. All of this information is printed to the user and charts are generated. Finally, if there are saved statistics from a previous run, the two benchmark runs are compared.\\n## Comparison\\nIn the comparison phase, the statistics calculated from the current benchmark run are compared against those saved by the previous run to determine if the performance has changed in the meantime, and if so, by how much.\\nOnce again, Criterion.rs generates many bootstrap samples, based on the measured samples from the two runs. The new and old bootstrap samples are compared and their T score is calculated using a T-test. The fraction of the bootstrapped T scores which are more extreme than the T score calculated by comparing the two measured samples gives the probability that the observed difference between the two sets of samples is merely by chance. Thus, if that probability is very low or zero, Criterion.rs can be confident that there is truly a difference in execution time between the two samples. In that case, the mean and median differences are bootstrapped and printed for the user, and the entire process begins again with the next benchmark.\\nThis process can be extremely sensitive to changes, especially when combined with a small, highly deterministic benchmark routine. In these circumstances even very small changes (eg. differences in the load from background processes) can change the measurements enough that the comparison process detects an optimization or regression. Since these sorts of unpredictable fluctuations are rarely of interest while benchmarking, there is also a configurable noise threshold. Optimizations or regressions within (for example) +-1% are considered noise and ignored. It is best to benchmark on a quiet computer where possible to minimize this noise, but it is not always possible to eliminate it entirely.\"}]"}},"session_id":"25f4c0a9-4d6f-40d6-8add-b5a829af0b4c","parent_tool_use_id":null,"uuid":"f2b7182a-65ed-4bd1-9750-27027dd6d8f7"}

These options are documented here.\\n\\n## Configuring Sample Count & Other Statistical Settings\\n\\nCriterion.rs allows the user to adjust certain statistical parameters. The most common way to set\\nthese is using the `BenchmarkGroup` structure - see the documentation for that structure for a list\\nof which settings are available.\\n\\n```\\n```\\n#![allow(unused)]\\nfn main() {\\nuse criterion::*;\\n\\nfn my_function() {\\n    ...\\n}\\n\\nfn bench(c: &mut Criterion) {\\n    let mut group = c.benchmark_group(\\\"sample-size-example\\\");\\n    // Configure Criterion.rs to detect smaller differences and increase sample size to improve\\n    // precision and counteract the resulting noise.\\n    group.significance_level(0.1).sample_size(500);\\n    group.bench_function(\\\"my-function\\\", |b| b.iter(|| my_function());\\n    group.finish();\\n}\\n\\ncriterion_group!(benches, bench);\\ncriterion_main!(benches);\\n}\\n```\\n```\\n\\nIt is also possible to change Criterion.rs' default values for these settings, by using the full\\nform of the `criterion_group` macro:\\n\\n```\\n```\\n#![allow(unused)]\\nfn main() {\\nuse criterion::*;\\n\\nfn my_function() {\\n    ...\\n}\\n\\nfn bench(c: &mut Criterion) {\\n    let mut group = c.benchmark_group(\\\"sample-size-example\\\");\\n    group.bench_function(\\\"my-function\\\", |b| b.iter(|| my_function());\\n    group.finish();\\n}\\n\\ncriterion_group!{\\n    name = benches;\\n    // This can be any expression that returns a `Criterion` object.\\n    config = Criterion::default().significance_level(0.1).sample_size(500);\\n    targets = bench\\n}\\ncriterion_main!(benches);\\n}\\n```\\n```\\n\\n## Throughput Measurements\\n\\nWhen benchmarking some types of code it is useful to measure the throughput as well as the iteration time, either in bytes per second or elements per second. Criterion.rs can estimate the throughput of a benchmark, but it needs to know how many bytes or elements each iteration will process.\\n\\nThroughput measurements are only supported when using the `BenchmarkGroup` structure; it is not available when using the simpler `bench_function` interface.\\n\\nTo measure throughput, use the `throughput` method on `BenchmarkGroup`, like so:\\n\\n```\\n```\\n#![allow(unused)]\\nfn main() {\\nuse criterion::*;\\n\\nfn decode(bytes: &[u8]) {\\n    // Decode the bytes\\n    ...\\n}\\n\\nfn bench(c: &mut Criterion) {\\n    let bytes : &[u8] = ...;\\n\\n    let mut group = c.benchmark_group(\\\"throughput-example\\\");\\n    group.throughput(Throughput::Bytes(bytes.len() as u64));\\n    group.bench_function(\\\"decode\\\", |b| b.iter(|| decode(bytes));\\n    group.finish();\\n}\\n\\ncriterion_group!(benches, bench);\\ncriterion_main!(benches);\\n}\\n```\\n```\\n\\nFor parameterized benchmarks, you can simply call the throughput function inside a loop:\\n\\n```\\n```\\n#![allow(unused)]\\nfn main() {\\nuse criterion::*;\\n\\ntype Element = ...;\\n\\nfn encode(elements: &[Element]) {\\n    // Encode the elements\\n    ...\\n}\\n\\nfn bench(c: &mut Criterion) {\\n    let elements_1 : &[u8] = ...;\\n    let elements_2 : &[u8] = ...;\\n\\n    let mut group = c.benchmark_group(\\\"throughput-example\\\");\\n    for (i, elements) in [elements_1, elements_2].iter().enumerate() {\\n        group.throughput(Throughput::Elements(elems.len() as u64));\\n        group.bench_with_input(format!(\\\"Encode {}\\\", i), elements, |elems, b| {\\n            b.iter(||encode(elems))\\n        });\\n    }\\n    group.finish();\\n}\\n\\ncriterion_group!(benches, bench);\\ncriterion_main!(benches);\\n}\\n```\\n```\\n\\nSetting the throughput causes a throughput estimate to appear in the output:\\n\\n```\\nalloc                   time:   [5.9846 ms 6.0192 ms 6.0623 ms]\\n                        thrpt:  [164.95 MiB/s 166.14 MiB/s 167.10 MiB/s]\\n```\\n\\n## Chart Axis Scaling\\n\\nBy default, Criterion.rs generates plots using a linear-scale axis. When using parameterized benchmarks, it is common for the input sizes to scale exponentially in order to cover a wide range of possible inputs. In this situation, it may be easier to read the resulting plots with a logarithmic axis.\\n\\nAs with throughput measurements above, this option is only available when using the `BenchmarkGroup` structure.\\n\\n```\\n```\\n#![allow(unused)]\\nfn main() {\\nuse criterion::*;\\n\\nfn do_a_thing(x: u64) {\\n    // Do something\\n    ...\\n}\\n\\nfn bench(c: &mut Criterion) {\\n    let plot_config = PlotConfiguration::default()\\n        .summary_scale(AxisScale::Logarithmic);\\n\\n    let mut group = c.benchmark_group(\\\"log_scale_example\\\");\\n    group.plot_config(plot_config);\\n    \\n    for i in [1u64, 10u64, 100u64, 1000u64, 10000u64, 100000u64, 1000000u64].iter() {\\n        group.bench_function(BenchmarkId::from_parameter(i), i, |b, i| b.iter(|| do_a_thing(i)));\\n    }\\n    group.finish();\\n}\\n\\ncriterion_group!(benches, bench);\\ncriterion_main!(benches);\\n}\\n```\\n```\\n\\nCurrently the axis scaling is the only option that can be set on the\\nPlotConfiguration struct. More may be added in the future.\\n\\n## Sampling Mode\\n\\nBy default, Criterion.rs can scale well to handle benchmarks that execute in picoseconds up to\\nbenchmarks that execute in milliseconds. Benchmarks that take longer will work just fine, but they\\ntend to take a long time to run. The only way to deal with this was to reduce the sample count.\\n\\nIn Criterion.rs 0.3.3, a new option was added to change the sampling mode to handle long-running\\nbenchmarks. The benchmark author can call `BenchmarkGroup::sampling_mode(SamplingMode)` to change\\nthe sampling mode.\\n\\nCurrently three options are available:\\n\\n- `SamplingMode::Auto`, which chooses a sampling mode from the other options automatically. This is the default.\\n- `SamplingMode::Linear`, the original sampling mode intended for faster benchmarks.\\n- `SamplingMode::Flat`, intended for long-running benchmarks.\\n\\nThe Flat sampling mode does change some of the statistical analysis and the charts that are\\ngenerated. This provides a way to filter\\nout some of these false positives at the cost of making it harder to detect small changes\\nto the true performance of the benchmark.\\n\\nThe default is 0.01, meaning that changes smaller than 1% will be ignored.\\n\\n##### §Panics\\n\\nPanics if the threshold is set to a negative value\\n\\nSource\\n\\nChanges the default confidence level for benchmarks run with this runner. The 0.95 value commonly referenced in Criterion.rs is the **confidence level** for statistical analysis, not a percentile measurement.\n\n## Key Findings\n\n### 1. Confidence Level vs. Percentiles\n\n**Confidence Level (0.95 default):**\n- This is a statistical parameter for confidence intervals\n- Represents the probability that the true runtime lies within the estimated interval\n- Default: 0.95 (95% confidence)\n- Configurable via `Criterion::confidence_level(f64)` or `BenchmarkGroup::confidence_level(f64)`\n- Range: (0, 1)\n\n**What Criterion.rs actually reports:**\n- Mean and median with confidence intervals\n- Standard deviation and median absolute deviation (MAD)\n- Throughput (if configured)\n- **NOT** p95, p99, or other percentile latencies\n\n### 2. Percentiles in Outlier Detection Only\n\nCriterion.rs uses percentiles **solely for outlier detection** using a modified Tukey's Method:\n- 25th percentile (Q1)\n- 75th percentile (Q3)\n- Interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 - Q1\n\nOutlier fences:\n- Mild outliers: Q1 - 1.5×IQR or Q3 + 1.5×IQR\n- Severe outliers: Q1 - 3×IQR or Q3 + 3×IQR\n\n**Important:** Outlier samples are NOT dropped from analysis—they are included in calculations but flagged in warnings and plots.\n\n### 3. Configurable Statistical Parameters\n\nAvailable configuration options on `Criterion` and `BenchmarkGroup`:\n\n| Parameter | Default | Description |\n|-----------|---------|-------------|\n| `confidence_level` | 0.95 | Probability that true value lies within confidence interval |\n| `significance_level` | 0.05 | Probability that identical code registers as 'different' due to noise |\n| `noise_threshold` | 0.01 (1%) | Changes smaller than this are ignored as noise |\n| `sample_size` | 100 | Number of measurements (minimum: 10) |\n| `measurement_time` | 5s | Duration for collecting measurements |\n| `warm_up_time` | 3s | Duration for warmup phase |\n| `resamples` | 100,000 | Number of bootstrap resamples |\n| `throughput` | None | Throughput measurement (bytes or elements per second) |\n\n### 4. Output Format Options\n\nCriterion.rs supports multiple output formats via `--output-format` CLI option:\n\n- **`criterion`** (default): Detailed statistical output with plots\n- **`bencher`**: Simplified format similar to nightly libtest benchmarks\n\nNeither format provides percentile latency output.\n\n### 5. Version Compatibility\n\nNEEDLE currently uses: `criterion = \"0.5\"` (dev-dependencies)\n\nMSRV: 1.75 (from rust-toolchain.toml) — Criterion 0.5 is compatible.\n\n## Configuration Approach for NEEDLE\n\nSince Criterion.rs does not provide p95 percentiles, there are two options:\n\n### Option A: Use Statistical Parameters as Proxy\n- Configure `confidence_level` to desired level (e.g., 0.95 for 95% confidence)\n- Monitor median and MAD as robust central tendency metrics\n- Use outlier detection as a proxy for tail behavior\n\n```rust\nlet mut group = c.benchmark_group(\"my-bench\");\ngroup.confidence_level(0.95);  // Already the default\ngroup.sample_size(500);         // Increase for better precision\n```\n\n### Option B: External Analysis\n- Export Criterion.rs raw data (stored in `target/criterion/`)\n- Parse and compute percentiles separately using `ndarray` or similar\n- Recommended for projects requiring true p95/p99 latency reporting\n\n## Sources\n\n- [Criterion.rs Analysis Process Documentation](https://bheisler.github.io/criterion.rs/book/analysis.html)\n- [Advanced Configuration - Criterion.rs](https://bheisler.github.io/criterion.rs/book/user_guide/advanced_configuration.html)\n- [Criterion Struct Documentation](https://docs.rs/criterion/latest/criterion/struct.Criterion.html)\n- [CHANGELOG.md - Criterion.rs](https://github.com/bheisler/criterion.rs/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md)\n\n## Conclusion\n\nCriterion.rs focuses on **statistical confidence intervals** for mean/median, not percentile distributions. The 0.95 value is a confidence level for interval estimation, not a percentile measurement. The library focuses on confidence intervals, mean/median statistics, and bootstrap resampling - not specific percentiles.\n\nTo get p95/p99 percentiles, you must calculate them manually from raw samples (which the existing `benches/sanitize.rs` already does correctly).\n\n## Criterion.rs Version in NEEDLE\n\nFrom `Cargo.toml`:\n```toml\n[dev-dependencies]\ncriterion = \"0.5\"\n```\n\n**Version:** 0.5 (current stable version as of 2026-07-02)\n\n**MSRV Compatibility:** Criterion 0.5 requires Rust 1.75+, which matches NEEDLE's MSRV of 1.75.\n\n## What Criterion.rs Actually Reports\n\nBased on the [Command-Line Output documentation](https://bheisler.github.io/criterion.rs/book/user_guide/command_line_output.html), Criterion.rs reports:\n\n### 1. Time Confidence Interval\n```\nalloc time: [2.5094 ms 2.5306 ms 2.5553 ms]\n```\n- Three values: `[lower_bound, estimate, upper_bound]`\n- Uses **bootstrap resampling** (100,000 samples by default)\n- Default confidence level: **95%** (configurable via `confidence_level()`)\n\n### 2. Mean and Standard Deviation\n```\nmean [2.5142 ms 2.5557 ms] std. dev. [62.868 us 149.50 us]\n```\n- Confidence interval for mean and std. dev.\n- Calculated naively from samples\n\n### 3. Median and Median Absolute Deviation\n```\nmedian [2.5023 ms 2.5262 ms] med. abs. dev. [40.034 us 73.259 us]\n```\n- **Robust statistics** - less sensitive to outliers than mean/std. dev.\n- Uses bootstrap resampling\n\n### 4. Slope (Linear Regression)\n```\nslope [2.5094 ms 2.5553 ms] R^2 [0.8660614 0.8640630]\n```\n- Time per iteration from linear regression\n- R² indicates goodness-of-fit\n\n### 5. Outlier Detection\n```\nFound 8 outliers among 100 measurements (8.00%)\n4 (4.00%) high mild\n4 (4.00%) high severe\n```\n- Uses modified Tukey's method (IQR-based)\n- Does NOT drop outliers from analysis\n\n### 6. Change Detection\n```\nchange: [-38.292% -37.342% -36.524%] (p = 0.00 < 0.05)\nPerformance has improved.\n```\n- Compares against previous run (stored in `target/criterion/`)\n- Statistical significance testing via T-test\n\n## Configuration Options Available\n\nFrom the [Criterion struct documentation](https://docs.rs/criterion/latest/criterion/struct.Criterion.html):\n\n| Method | Description | Default |\n|--------|-------------|---------|\n| `confidence_level(f64)` | Confidence interval width (0.95 = 95%) | 0.95 |\n| `sample_size(usize)` | Number of measurements (min 10) | 100 |\n| `measurement_time(Duration)` | How long to collect samples | 5 seconds |\n| `warm_up_time(Duration)` | Warmup duration | 3 seconds |\n| `noise_threshold(f64)` | Ignore changes smaller than this | 0.01 (1%) |\n| `significance_level(f64)` | Threshold for change detection | 0.05 |\n| `nresamples(usize)` | Bootstrap sample count | 100,000 |\n\n### Example Configuration\n```rust\nfn configure_criterion() -> Criterion {\n    Criterion::default()\n        .confidence_level(0.95)\n        .sample_size(100)\n        .warm_up_time(std::time::Duration::from_secs(3))\n        .measurement_time(std::time::Duration::from_secs(5))\n        .noise_threshold(0.02)\n}\n```\n\n## Why Criterion.rs Doesn't Report p95/p99\n\nCriterion.rs is designed for **statistical comparison** between runs, not latency SLA reporting:\n\n- **Focus:** Detecting performance regressions/improvements between code versions\n- **Method:** Bootstrap resampling + confidence intervals + hypothesis testing\n- **Assumption:** Normal-ish distribution (or at least symmetric)\n\n**p95/p99 percentiles** are more relevant for:\n- SLA compliance (\"99% of requests under 100ms\")\n- Highly-skewed distributions (latency outliers)\n- Tail latency analysis\n\nThese are different use cases than what Criterion.rs targets.\n\n## How to Get p95/p99 Percentiles\n\n### Approach 1: Manual Calculation (Current NEEDLE Approach)\n\nThe existing `benches/sanitize.rs` already implements this correctly in `bench_median_latency()`:\n\n```rust\nfn bench_median_latency(c: &mut Criterion) {\n    let sanitizer = Sanitizer::new(&[]).expect(\"failed to build sanitizer\");\n    let content = generate_trace_content(SIZE_100KB);\n\n    // Warm-up\n    for _ in 0..5 {\n        let _ = sanitizer.sanitize(&content);\n    }\n\n    // Collect samples\n    let mut latencies = Vec::with_capacity(ASSERTION_SAMPLE_COUNT);\n    for _ in 0..ASSERTION_SAMPLE_COUNT {\n        let start = std::time::Instant::now();\n        let _ = sanitizer.sanitize(&content);\n        latencies.push(start.elapsed().as_micros());\n    }\n\n    // Calculate percentiles\n    latencies.sort();\n    let median_us = latencies[ASSERTION_SAMPLE_COUNT / 2];\n    let p95_us = latencies[(latencies.len() * 95) / 100];\n    let p99_us = latencies[(latencies.len() * 99) / 100];\n\n    eprintln!(\"Median: {:.2} ms\", median_us as f64 / 1000.0);\n    eprintln!(\"P95: {:.2} ms\", p95_us as f64 / 1000.0);\n    eprintln!(\"P99: {:.2} ms\", p99_us as f64 / 1000.0);\n}\n```\n\n### Approach 2: Post-Process Criterion Output\n\nCriterion.rs saves raw sample data to `target/criterion/<name>/raw.csv`. You can:\n\n1. Run benchmarks with Criterion\n2. Parse `raw.csv` to extract measurements\n3. Calculate percentiles with external tools (Python, R, etc.)\n\n### Approach 3: Use Alternative Libraries\n\nFor projects that need built-in p95/p99:\n- **[divan](https://github.com/magnet/tragnet)**: Focus on percentiles\n- **[rack](https://github.com/snipe/rack)**: Latency-focused benchmarking\n- Custom: Simple timing loop with manual percentile calc\n\n## Existing NEEDLE Configuration Analysis\n\nThe current `benches/sanitize.rs` configuration (lines 46-53):\n\n```rust\nfn configure_criterion() -> Criterion {\n    Criterion::default()\n        .confidence_level(0.95)    // ✓ Correct for CI width\n        .sample_size(100)            // ✓ Reasonable for percentiles\n        .warm_up_time(std::time::Duration::from_secs(3))\n        .measurement_time(std::time::Duration::from_secs(5))\n        .noise_threshold(0.02)\n}\n```\n\n**Assessment:** This configuration is **appropriate** for the current use case:\n\n- ✓ `confidence_level(0.95)` - Sets 95% confidence interval width (not percentile)\n- ✓ `sample_size(100)` - Provides reasonable accuracy for bootstrap statistics\n- ✓ Manual p95 calculation in `bench_median_latency()` - Correct approach\n\n## Documentation References\n\n- [Criterion.rs Analysis Process](https://bheisler.github.io/criterion.rs/book/analysis.html) - Bootstrap resampling methodology\n- [Criterion.rs Command-Line Output](https://bheisler.github.io/criterion.rs/book/user_guide/command_line_output.html) - Output format explained\n- [Criterion.rs Documentation (docs.rs)](https://docs.rs/criterion/latest/criterion/struct.Criterion.html) - API reference\n\n## Conclusions\n\n1. **Criterion.rs 0.5 is the correct version** for NEEDLE (matches MSRV 1.75)\n\n2. **Criterion.rs does not have built-in p95/p99 output** - it reports:\n   - Mean/std. dev. with confidence intervals\n   - Median/med. abs. dev. with confidence intervals\n   - Outlier detection\n   - Change detection vs previous run\n\n3. **Configuration approach for p95**:\n   - **Correct**: Manual calculation from raw samples (current approach in `benches/sanitize.rs`)\n   - **Misconception**: `confidence_level(0.95)` controls confidence interval width, NOT percentile reporting\n\n4. **Existing NEEDLE code is correct** - The `configure_criterion()` function and `bench_median_latency()` implement the right approach:\n   - Use Criterion for general benchmark statistics and regression detection\n   - Manually calculate p95/p99 from raw samples for latency reporting\n\n## Recommendations\n\nThe current implementation in `benches/sanitize.rs` is **already correct** and does not need changes for p95 reporting.
